sources.note: Nothing. States the language is 'not sufficiently attested to classify'; the only recorded word is 'Yanaguana' (village/river name) from Damian Massanet's diary, 13 June 1691.

sources.citation: Campbell, T. N. & T. J. Campbell. 1985. Indian Groups Associated with Spanish Missions of the San Antonio Missions National Historical Park. Center for Archaeological Research, The University of Texas at San Antonio, Special Report No. 16. [NPS History e-text edition]
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. The Payaya entry is one paragraph of mission demography and territory plus one sentence on language: 'A few words believed to be of Payaya origin seem to indicate that the Payaya spoke a dialect of the Coahuilteco language (Goddard 1979:366-367).' The only 'stress'/'phonetic' tokens in the whole report are 'It must be stressed that the Spanish documents..' and 'depending upon the phonetic complexity of the name' (on Spanish spellings of group names).

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1940. Linguistic Material from the Tribes of Southern Texas and Northeastern Mexico. Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 127. Washington: GPO. (Glottolog ref 62513; listed by Glottolog as an overview;minimal; language code Payaya, Aranama, San Francisco Solano)
sources.note: Nothing. Payaya appears three times: p. 5 'We also have a single word from the tongue of the Payaya who lived on or near the Rio San Antonio'; p. 55 (Additional Coahuilteco words from the mission records) 'yana wana (yana guana), the San Antonio River. In the language of the Payaya tribe which lived upon it.'; p. 135 in the conjectural list of Coahuiltecan bands. No accent marks, no phonology, no wordlist (the earlier scan note's '25-item wordlist' is wrong: it is one word).

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1915. Linguistic Position of the Tribes of Southern Texas and Northeastern Mexico. American Anthropologist n.s. 17(1): 17-40.
sources.note: No phonology for Payaya. The only Payaya content (pp. 35-36) gives yana guana as the Payaya name of the San Antonio River with guana = Coahuilteco 'water'. No accent marks, no stress or tone remark; the rest is lexical comparison of Coahuilteco, Comecrudo, Cotoname, Karankawa, Tonkawa, Atakapa.
